course.title: AP U.S. History
course.description: Trace how Americans have argued over identity, power, work, and their place in the world, from the societies that existed before 1491 to the present.
course.previewDescription: Follow the nation's development from early contact and colonization through independence, civil war, industrialization, world wars, and recent decades.

unit.title: Period 5
unit.description: Follow Manifest Destiny and the Mexican–American War, the sectional conflict over slavery, the election of 1860 and secession, the Civil War, and Reconstruction and its failure from 1844 to 1877.

framework.name: Course themes
framework.title: Use the course themes to choose your evidence
framework.intro: The themes connect developments across all nine periods. A piece of evidence can fit more than one theme; choose the one that answers the prompt.
framework.sourceNote: Theme names, codes, and descriptions follow the AP U.S. History Course and Exam Description (fall 2026).

themes.title: American and National Identity
themes.description: This theme focuses on how and why definitions of American and national identity and values have developed among the diverse and changing population of North America as well as on related topics, such as citizenship, constitutionalism, foreign policy, assimilation, and American exceptionalism.
themes.question: Who counted as American, and what did people believe the nation stood for?
themes.example: Debates over ratifying the Constitution turned on what kind of republic Americans wanted.

themes.title: Work, Exchange, and Technology
themes.description: This theme focuses on the factors behind the development of systems of economic exchange, particularly the role of technology, economic markets, and government.
themes.question: How did people earn a living, trade, and use new technology?
themes.example: Canals and railroads tied farmers in the West to markets in the East.

themes.title: Geography and the Environment
themes.description: This theme focuses on the role of geography and both the natural and human-made environments in the social and political developments in what would become the United States.
themes.question: How did land, climate, and resources shape choices, and how did people change them?
themes.example: The Chesapeake's climate suited tobacco, which shaped its labor system.

themes.title: Migration and Settlement
themes.description: This theme focuses on why and how the various people who moved to and within the United States both adapted to and transformed their new social and physical environments.
themes.question: Why did people move, and how did they change the places they settled?
themes.example: The Great Migration brought African Americans from the rural South to northern cities.

themes.title: Politics and Power
themes.description: This theme focuses on how different social and political groups have influenced society and government in the United States as well as how political beliefs and institutions have changed over time.
themes.question: Who held power, how did they use it, and who challenged it?
themes.example: The New Deal expanded the federal government's role in the economy.

themes.title: America in the World
themes.description: This theme focuses on the interactions between nations that affected North American history in the colonial period and on the influence of the United States on world affairs.
themes.question: How did contact, trade, diplomacy, and war connect America to other nations?
themes.example: The Seven Years' War left Britain in debt and changed its policies toward the colonies.

themes.title: American and Regional Culture
themes.description: This theme focuses on the how and why national, regional, and group cultures developed and changed as well as how culture has shaped government policy and the economy.
themes.question: How did beliefs, religion, arts, and media develop and shape public life?
themes.example: The Second Great Awakening inspired many Americans to join reform movements.

themes.title: Social Structures
themes.description: This theme focuses on how and why systems of social organization develop and change as well as the impact that these systems have on the broader society.
themes.question: How were people ranked by race, class, and gender, and how did that change?
themes.example: The growth of a middle class in the Gilded Age changed ideas about leisure and family.

quiz.title: Unit 5 SAQ 02
quiz.headline: Hayes's Inaugural Address
quiz.prompt: Using the sources above, answer (a), (b), and (c).
quiz.instructions: Answer (a), (b), and (c). Each part is worth one point. Answer the question directly, support it with specific historical evidence, and explain how the evidence supports your answer. Describe means more than mentioning a term; explain means showing how or why.
quiz.note: Original Page One practice in AP format. Rubric criteria follow the College Board's AP history rubrics; scoring here is your own self-assessment, not an official score.

stimulusBlocks.source: CED Topic 5.11, KC-5.3.II.E: segregation, violence, Supreme Court decisions, and local political tactics progressively stripped away African American rights
stimulusBlocks.attribution: President Rutherford B. Hayes, in his Inaugural Address on March 5, 1877, after a disputed election and as federal troops were leaving the last Southern states they occupied
stimulusBlocks.citation: Rutherford B. Hayes, Inaugural Address (March 5, 1877). NLTK inaugural corpus, 1877-Hayes.txt.
stimulusBlocks.note: Hayes uses “local self-government” to mean that Southern states would run their own affairs without federal troops. “The white and … the colored people” means white and Black Southerners.
stimulusBlocks.text:
The people of those States are still impoverished, and the inestimable blessing of wise, honest, and peaceful local self-government is not fully enjoyed. Whatever difference of opinion may exist as to the cause of this condition of things, the fact is clear that in the progress of events the time has come when such government is the imperative necessity required by all the varied interests, public and private, of those States. But it must not be forgotten that only a local government which recognizes and maintains inviolate the rights of all is a true self-government.

Let me assure my countrymen of the Southern States that it is my earnest desire to regard and promote their truest interest -- the interests of the white and of the colored people both and equally -- and to put forth my best efforts in behalf of a civil policy which will forever wipe out in our political affairs the color line and the distinction between North and South, to the end that we may have not merely a united North or a united South, but a united country.

scaffold.label: Answer
scaffold.text: Respond directly to the task verb: identify, describe, explain, or compare.

scaffold.label: Prove
scaffold.text: Name a specific event, development, or circumstance from the period in the prompt.

scaffold.label: Explain
scaffold.text: Show how or why the evidence answers the question.

parts.prompt: Briefly describe ONE goal for the South that President Hayes expresses in the excerpt.
criteria: Identifies a goal stated in the excerpt, such as local self-government or national reunion.
Uses the excerpt to show it, with more than a copied phrase.

model.answer: Hayes sought local self-government in the Southern states that would also protect the rights of all.
model.prove: He calls “wise, honest, and peaceful local self-government” the “imperative necessity” of those states, and says that only a government that “maintains inviolate the rights of all is a true self-government.”
model.explain: The goal signaled the end of federal intervention in the South, because the states would manage their own affairs, and Hayes promised that the rights of both white and Black Southerners would still be respected.

parts.alternatives: A response can also point to his hope to “wipe out in our political affairs the color line and the distinction between North and South” for “a united country,” if it explains that he sought reconciliation between the sections.

review.label: Redeemers, violence, and the end of Reconstruction

parts.prompt: Briefly explain ONE specific historical development from 1865 to 1877 that contributed to the end of Reconstruction.
criteria: Explains how it weakened or ended Reconstruction.

model.answer: Violence and intimidation by white Southerners who opposed Reconstruction contributed to its end.
model.prove: Groups such as the Ku Klux Klan, the White League, and the Red Shirts attacked Black voters and Republican officials, and by 1876 Democrats called Redeemers had regained control of most Southern state governments.
model.explain: The violence kept Black voters from the polls and weakened Republican governments, while Northern support for sending troops faded, so Reconstruction could no longer be enforced.

parts.alternatives: A response can also use the Panic of 1873 and the scandals of Grant's administration, which turned Northern attention away from the South, or the Compromise of 1877, if it explains how the development ended federal enforcement.

review.label: Redeemers, violence, and the end of Reconstruction

parts.prompt: Briefly explain ONE way that the rights or economic independence of African Americans in the South were limited after 1877.
criteria: Names a specific limit on rights or economic independence after 1877.
Explains how it limited African Americans.

model.answer: Sharecropping limited the economic independence of formerly enslaved people.
model.prove: Planters still owned most of the land, and freed families farmed plots for a share of the crop, bought supplies on credit at high prices, and often owed more than the crop was worth.
model.explain: The debts bound families to the land and to the planters, so they fell short of the self-sufficiency that they had sought through land ownership.

parts.alternatives: A response can also use poll taxes and literacy tests, Jim Crow laws, the Supreme Court decisions in the Civil Rights Cases or Plessy v. Ferguson, or violence, if it explains how the tactic limited African American rights.
